---
title: "What RL Actually Does to a Model, and Where It's Heading"
---

Parts I to III asked what each method optimizes. This chapter asks what the optimization does to the
model. Does RL teach a pretrained model anything new, or does it only make it more reliable at what it
could already do? Does it generalize better or worse than supervised fine-tuning? What does it cost in
diversity, and in forgetting? These questions became urgent with the reasoning models of 2025, and the
evidence is genuinely mixed. The chapter presents it as a debate and keeps three kinds of claim apart:
mathematical facts, findings that several groups have replicated, and claims that are recent or
contested. Where the toy language can settle a mathematical point it does, and where it cannot, the
chapter says so. The last section turns to the setting where the classical RL of the
[first chapter](01-what-makes-a-problem-rl.qmd) returns in full: multi-turn, tool-using agents. It is
date-stamped, because it is the part of the field that moves fastest.

## Sharpening or new capability?

**The finding.** Yue et al. compared reasoning models trained with RL on verifiable rewards (RLVR)
against their own base models using pass@$k$, the probability that at least one of $k$ samples is
correct. "RLVR-trained models outperform their base models at small $k$ (e.g., $k = 1$)", but "the base
models achieve a higher pass@$k$ score when $k$ is large", and the reasoning paths of the RL models
were already in the base models' sampling distribution; they conclude that the reasoning abilities
"originate from and are bounded by the base model" [@yue2025does]. On this reading, RLVR mostly
*sharpens*: it moves probability onto good answers the base model could already sample, which helps
when you get one try and hurts when you get many.

**The counter-evidence.** Liu et al.'s ProRL trains much longer, with KL control, periodic resets of the
reference policy and a diverse task suite, and reports that "RL-trained models consistently outperform
base models across a wide range of pass@$k$ evaluations", including where the base model fails
completely; the improvement correlates with the base model's competence on the task and with training
duration [@liu2025prorl]. So the boundary may move with enough optimization and the right recipe, or
the two papers may be measuring different regimes. As of October 2026 this is a **contested** question,
and both papers should be read as reports about their settings.

**What the mathematics says.** One part of the debate is not empirical. For a single problem with
success probability $p$, pass@$k = 1 - (1-p)^k$ is increasing in $p$ for every $k$. So if RL raises the
success rate on a problem, it raises pass@$k$ on that problem *at every $k$*. A crossover in which the
RL model's pass@$k$ falls below the base model's at large $k$ is possible only if RL has *lowered* the
success rate on some problems, enough to outweigh the gains on others. Sharpening by itself does not
produce it; losing problems does.

The toy language shows both halves (@fig-pass-at-k). With a fully expressive policy per prompt, the
KL-regularized optimum $\pi^\star_\beta$ raises every prompt's success rate, and its pass@$k$ lies above
the reference policy's at every $k$ for every $\beta$. To get a crossover the toy needs something that
can make RL lower a problem's success rate. The simplest such thing is shared capacity: one
distribution that must serve five tasks whose correct answers compete, with the tasks appearing in
training at different frequencies. That is deliberately extreme (a real model sees the prompt and can
specialize), but it isolates the mechanism. RL moves the shared distribution toward what is rewarded
most often. Frequency-weighted pass@1 doubles, from 0.20 to 0.40, while the success rate on the three
rarest tasks falls to zero, so pass@256 drops from 1.0 to 0.42 for the unregularized RL policy. The
KL-regularized optima show the same pattern more gently as $\beta$ falls.

![Left: on the default testbed, with a separate (fully expressive) policy for each prompt, the KL-regularized optimum raises pass@$k$ at every $k$. Middle: one shared distribution serving five tasks that appear in training with frequencies 40/30/15/10/5%; as optimization strengthens (smaller $\beta$, or RLOO with no KL), pass@1 rises but pass@$k$ at large $k$ falls below the base, a crossover. Right: why: success moves to the frequently rewarded task and vanishes on the others. All values exact.](../images/pass_at_k.png){#fig-pass-at-k}

The toy cannot say which mechanism operates in real models: shared parameters, a narrowing of the
reasoning strategies a model will try, or the KL-free, long optimization of recent recipes. What it
pins down is the logical structure of the question. **A pass@$k$ crossover is evidence that RL lowered
success on some problems, not merely that it sharpened the distribution on all of them.**

## Generalization and memorization

Chu et al. compare SFT and RL on two tasks built to test generalization: GeneralPoints, an arithmetic
card game with rule variants, and V-IRL, a real-world navigation environment. Their abstract: "RL,
especially when trained with an outcome-based reward, generalizes across both rule-based textual and
visual variants", while "SFT, in contrast, tends to memorize training data and struggles to generalize
out-of-distribution scenarios" [@chu2025sft]. Two qualifications travel with the result. SFT is not dispensable in their pipeline:
"SFT stabilizes the model's output format, enabling subsequent RL to achieve its performance gains"
[@chu2025sft]. And the tasks are specific environments, not general language-model training. Kirk et
al. found the same direction for RLHF on text, "RLHF generalises better than SFT to new inputs,
particularly as the distribution shift between train and test becomes larger" [@kirk2023understanding].
Two groups, different settings, the same direction: this is the closest the section comes to a
**replicated finding**, with the caveat that "generalizes better" was measured on particular kinds of
distribution shift.

A first-principles reading is available from the earlier chapters, and it is a reading, not a proof.
SFT fits the forward KL to a fixed dataset of someone else's responses
([keeping updates stable](03-keeping-updates-stable.qmd)), so it is rewarded for reproducing the
dataset's surface. RL is rewarded only for outcomes, on the model's own samples
([the first chapter](01-what-makes-a-problem-rl.qmd)), which is the DAgger remedy for imitation's
distribution shift ([the LLM-as-policy chapter](04-the-llm-as-a-policy.qmd)).

## Forgetting

Shenfeld, Pari and Agrawal ask why online RL seems to forget less of a model's prior abilities than
SFT when both learn a new task to the same level. Their answer, "RL's Razor": forgetting is predicted
by "the KL-divergence between the fine-tuned and base policy evaluated on the new task", and
"on-policy RL is implicitly biased towards KL-minimal solutions among the many that solve the new
task, whereas SFT can converge to distributions arbitrarily far from the base model" [@shenfeld2025razor].
This fits the structure of the book's methods. An on-policy method moves probability mass among
responses the current policy already produces, reweighting them, so the solution it finds is near
where it started. SFT moves the policy toward whatever distribution the labels came from, however far
away. The finding is recent (2025) and from one group, so it belongs with the **recent claims**; its
mechanism is consistent with the mathematics of the earlier chapters.

## Diversity collapse

The most consistently reported cost of RL is diversity. Kirk et al. found that "RLHF significantly
reduces output diversity compared to SFT across a variety of measures" [@kirk2023understanding].
Korbak et al. opened their argument for KL-regularized RL with the observation that standard RL
fine-tuning "leads to distribution collapse" [@korbak2022rl]. Yue et al.'s narrowing is a version of
the same thing seen through pass@$k$.

The book has met collapse three times, and each time it had an identifiable cause. Unregularized
REINFORCE collapsed onto a single correct answer while SFT kept the expert's spread
([the first chapter](01-what-makes-a-problem-rl.qmd)). Iterated hard filtering, the STaR/ReST pattern,
drove the entropy among correct answers to zero, well past even $\pi_{\text{ref}}$ restricted to correct
answers ([imitating a better distribution](09-imitating-a-better-distribution.qmd)). And the reverse KL
in the RL objective is mode-seeking ([keeping updates stable](03-keeping-updates-stable.qmd)). The
mathematical fact underneath all three: the KL-regularized optimum $\pi^\star$ keeps every response
$\pi_{\text{ref}}$ supports, in the same relative proportions within each reward level
([the shared-target chapter](06-the-shared-target.qmd)). Collapse comes from removing the KL term, from
optimizing past the point where it binds, from finite-sample feedback loops, or from a policy too
constrained to represent $\pi^\star$. It is not something the objective requires.

| Claim | Kind of evidence | Status as of October 2026 |
|---|---|---|
| Per problem, raising the success rate raises pass@$k$ at every $k$ | mathematical fact | settled |
| The KL-regularized optimum keeps $\pi_{\text{ref}}$'s support and proportions within each reward level | mathematical fact | settled |
| RL reduces output diversity relative to SFT | several groups (Kirk et al.; Korbak et al.; Yue et al.'s narrowing) | replicated |
| RL generalizes better than SFT under distribution shift | two groups, different settings (Chu et al.; Kirk et al.) | replicated, setting-dependent |
| RLVR does not expand what the base model can solve | Yue et al. vs. ProRL | contested |
| On-policy RL forgets less because it finds KL-minimal solutions | Shenfeld et al. | recent, single group |

## Where full RL comes back: multi-turn and agentic RL

*This section describes the field as of October 2026 and is deliberately short.*

The [chapter on the LLM as a policy](04-the-llm-as-a-policy.qmd) explained why LLM post-training could
drop so much of classical RL: deterministic transitions, a single reward at the end, a bandit over
responses. Every one of those properties fails for an agent. When a model calls tools, browses, runs
code or talks to a user over several turns, the next state depends on the environment's response,
which is stochastic and outside the model's control. Rewards arrive after many turns, and the turn that
earned them may be far back. The [first chapter's](01-what-makes-a-problem-rl.qmd) third property,
delayed consequences, returns at the level of turns rather than tokens, and with it the machinery of
values, bootstrapping and credit assignment.

::: {.callout-important title="Classical lineage — this is the full MDP again"}
Multi-turn agents restore everything the bandit view of single responses removed: stochastic
transitions, rewards delayed across decisions, and the need to estimate the value of intermediate
states. Values, bootstrapping and temporal credit assignment, the classical tools of the
[first chapter](01-what-makes-a-problem-rl.qmd), apply again, at the level of turns.
:::

The literature shows that machinery coming back. ArCHer argues that "most single-turn RL methods
cannot endow LLMs with the ability to intelligently seek information over multiple turns, perform
credit assignment, or reason about their past actions", and pairs an off-policy, value-based learner
over whole utterances with a token-level policy inside each turn [@zhou2024archer]: a critic again,
now at the level where consequences are delayed. RefGRPO finds that agents mis-assess their own outputs
after seeing environment feedback and adds a calibration bonus for their self-assessment
[@zhu2026reflection], a link to the [calibration chapter](10-rewarding-calibration.qmd). And reward
hacking takes environmental forms, such as exiting a test harness early or skipping tests in agentic
coding [@baker2025monitoring].

Systems matter more here too. Generation dominates the cost of RL for language models, and agentic
rollouts are longer and slower still, so practical systems decouple generation from learning and train
on slightly stale samples. Noukhovitch et al. study how much off-policyness that tolerates, and find
online DPO the most robust [@noukhovitch2025asynchronous]. This book does not cover rollout engines or
weight synchronization; it is enough to know that "on-policy" in an agentic system usually means "a
few versions behind", and that the importance ratios of the
[chapter on stable updates](03-keeping-updates-stable.qmd) are what make that workable.

## Connections

- [Keeping Updates Stable](03-keeping-updates-stable.qmd) explains the forward- vs. reverse-KL contrast
  behind diversity collapse and behind the generalization and forgetting findings.
- [The Shared Target, and RLHF with PPO](06-the-shared-target.qmd) supplies the mathematical fact that
  the regularized optimum does not collapse, so that collapse can be traced to what a recipe removed.
- [Learning by Imitating a Better Distribution](09-imitating-a-better-distribution.qmd) produced the
  clearest collapse in the book, from iterated filtering, the same self-training loop many reasoning
  recipes use.
- [The LLM as a Policy](04-the-llm-as-a-policy.qmd) listed which parts of classical RL LLM training
  could drop; the agentic section of this chapter is where they come back.
